newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Buba's Meister calls deficits EMU enemy No.1.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Buba's Meister calls deficits EMU enemy No.1.

text.p: Highlighting Germany's own difficulties in cutting debt levels, Bundesbank board member Edgar Meister said on Tuesday that budgetary consolidation was the top challenge facing the European Union.

Meister said one-off efforts to cut deficits were not enough to ensure lasting fiscal restraint and all German public authorities -- not just the federal government -- had to strive to meet the Maastricht criteria.
"Without doubt it must be acknowledged that by now all states are making a big effort to reduce their deficits," Meister said according to the text of a speech.
"But this process must not end with the one-off fulfilment of convergence criteria."
Meister's remarks come the day after the German government raised its forecast for the year's budget deficits to 2.9 percent of gross domestic product from 2.5 percent.

Although the figure is still under the Maastricht Treaty's three percent target, the revision shows that the budget deficit ratio is not shrinking as quickly as had been hoped, and fuelled wide-spread scepticism in financial markets as to whether Germany really would make the target level.
"Without the cooperation of the Laender (federal states) we will not succeed in keeping on course for consolidation," Meister said.
Some analysts fear that the difficulties Germany faces in slashing its deficit are adding pressure for a politically-driven "fudge" of the criteria.

But another Bundesbank council member Franz-Christoph Zeitler tried to limit the scope for such a watering down of the targets, using a speech in Munich to restate the Bundesbank determination to see Maastricht applied strictly.
Zeitler said the stability and trust aspects of Maastricht Treaty, must be "taken seriously, strictly applied and credibly fulfilled."

Zeitler, who is also president of the Bundesbank's regional office for Bavaria, added that a fall in interest rates among European nations at the same time their currencies have strengthened shows that markets were confident that the convergence criteria would be successfully met.
A summary of Zeitler's remarks was made available to the press.

Bundesbank vice-president Johann Wilhelm Gaddum, meanwhile, speaking about domestic economic matters, said the German central bank did not see grave risks for price developments, despite the dollar's recent surge against the mark and slightly stronger German inflation.
Gaddum told Germany's Handelsblatt daily newspaper that the Bundesbank saw "no price dangers that could have a severe impact on us".
The newspaper also quoted Gaddum as saying there was no reason to talk the dollar up or down from its present level.

The dollar has surged against the mark to around 1.65 marks from near 1.50 in November. A strong dollar, at least in theory, can be inflationary for Germany as the cost of some raw materials is priced in dollars.
On money supply, Bundesbank's prime policy indicator, Gaddum noted that money supply had risen by an annualised 5.9 percent in the last six months of 1996.
"So we were comfortably within our target range," he said. The Bundesbank was aiming for money supply growth of four to seven percent in 1996.
"If you take exchange rates into account, there is no particular reason to force the deutsche mark lower through interest rate reductions," the paper quoted him as saying.
